greek.etymology: Root: *leg- 'to collect, gather, speak'. English descendants: Logic (reasoning according to strict principles), Dialogue (conversation between two or more), Epilogue (concluding section of literary work), Catalogue (complete list of items)
greek.usage_example: τοῦ δὲ λόγου τοῦδ᾽ ἐόντος ἀεὶ ἀξύνετοι γίγνονται ἄνθρωποι — Of this Word's eternal being humans prove to be ignorant
greek.did_you_know: The Stoics distinguished between λόγος ἐνδιάθετος (internal thought) and λόγος προφορικός (spoken word). They believed the cosmic Logos was like divine internal thought made manifest in the physical world's rational order.

french.forms: Singular: un spleen, le spleen. Plural: des spleens (rare; Baudelaire uses it as uncountable)
french.etymology: From Greek: splḗn (σπλήν) — the organ itself. Medieval medicine believed the spleen produced black bile → melancholy. English adopted 'spleen' as emotional gloom (17th c.). Baudelaire re-imported it into French with darker connotations.
french.literary_context: Charles Baudelaire, Les Fleurs du Mal, 1857 — 'Spleen LXXVIII'
french.usage_example: Je suis un cimetière abhorré de la lune. — I am a graveyard abhorred by the moon.
french.did_you_know: Les Fleurs du Mal was prosecuted for obscenity upon publication in 1857 — same year as Madame Bovary's trial. Baudelaire lost. Six poems were legally suppressed and could not be published in France until 1949 — 82 years later.

german.meaning: Pain caused by the gap between the world as it is and as it should be — grief at existence itself.
german.forms: Singular only — no standard plural. Nom: der Weltschmerz, Acc: den Weltschmerz, Dat: dem Weltschmerz, Gen: des Weltschmerzes
german.etymology: Welt (world) ← Old High German 'weralt' ← wer (man) + alt (age) → cognate: English 'world'. Schmerz (pain, ache) ← Middle High German 'smerze' ← Proto-Germanic *smertaz → cognate: English 'smart' (as in stinging pain)
german.literary_context: Heinrich Heine, 'Die romantische Schule' (Der romantische Schule), 1836
german.usage_example: Aus meinem großen Schmerzen mach ich die kleinen Lieder. — From my great pain I make the small songs.
german.did_you_know: Heine's 'Die romantische Schule' (1836) was written in FRENCH first — for a Parisian audience — then self-translated into German. The book was banned in German states under the Carlsbad Decrees. Heine spent 25 years in Parisian exile, writing German literature.

oldenglish.forms: Base noun candel (fem., weak declension): Sg: candel / candlan / candlan / candlan; Pl: candlan / candlana / candlum / candlan
oldenglish.etymology: candel ← Latin candela ← candēre 'to shine'; woruld ← Proto-Germanic *weraldiz (*we-raldiz = 'age of man'). Old Norse cognate: veröld. The kenning itself has no Norse parallel — it's a West Germanic poetic coinage.
oldenglish.literary_context: Beowulf, c. 700–1000, line 1965 of the Cotton Vitellius A.xv manuscript. The compound appears once, in a dawn passage marking Beowulf's departure from Heorot.
oldenglish.did_you_know: Beowulf survives in a SINGLE manuscript: Cotton Vitellius A.xv, copied c. 1000 CE by two scribes whose hands change at line 1939 — near woruld-candel. The manuscript was almost destroyed in the 1731 Ashburnham House fire. Its edges remain scorched and brittle

latin.meaning: fate; that which has been spoken
latin.forms: SING: fātum / fātī / fātō / fātum / fāte / fātō; PLUR: fāta / fātōrum / fātīs / fāta / fāta / fātīs
latin.etymology: fātum ← faor/fārī (to speak) ← PIE *bʰeh₂- (to speak). Same root: Greek φημί (phēmí). Romance descendants: IT: fato | ES: hado | FR: fée (fairy). English: fate, fatal, fatality, infant (in-fans = not speaking)
latin.usage_example: fāto profugus — an exile by fate
latin.did_you_know: The Aeneid was unfinished when Virgil died in 19 BCE. He reportedly asked his literary executors Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca to burn it. Augustus intervened — the poem survived by imperial command.
